entry: Largest and most formal [[Meal|meal]] of the day in many Western cultures. Historically the largest meal was eaten around midday and was called dinner; among the elite it gradually moved later in the day over the 16th to 19th centuries. Reflecting the custom of the 17th century, [[Louis XIV]] dined at noon and had supper at 10:00 pm. In 1765 [[George III|King George III]] dined at 4:00 pm, and by about 1850 English middle-class dinners were around 5:00 or 6:00 pm. In modern usage dinner usually means the evening meal, typically the largest of the day, with earlier meals called [[Breakfast|breakfast]] and [[Lunch|lunch]]; supper is now often an alternative term for it. The word derives from Old French *disner*, from a Gallo-Romance term meaning "to break one's fast." It is still used for a meal at noon on special occasions, such as a Christmas dinner.

Mostly marine, unicellular [[Protist|protist]] with two [[Flagellum|flagella]]. The name combines Greek *dinos* ("whirling") and Latin *flagellum* ("whip"), describing the way they were seen to swim and their flagella. Dinoflagellates are mostly marine [[Plankton|plankton]], though many live in freshwater. Many are [[Photosynthesis|photosynthetic]], but a large fraction of these are mixotrophic, also ingesting prey, and others are unpigmented predators. Some species live inside marine animals and are important to the biology of [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. About 2,294 living species have been estimated, including marine, freshwater and parasitic forms. Rapid accumulations, known as red tides, can discolor water and cause shellfish poisoning in people who eat contaminated shellfish. Some species emit blue-green bioluminescence.

[[Roman emperor]] (r. 284–305). Born Diocles to a family of low status in Dalmatia, he rose through the army and was proclaimed emperor by the troops after the deaths of Carus and his son Numerian. He ended the [[Crisis of the Third Century|Crisis of the Third Century]] and in 293 created the Tetrarchy, or "rule of four," with Maximian as senior colleague and Galerius and Constantius as junior ones. He reorganized the provinces, separated the civil and military services, and standardized taxation. His Edict on Maximum Prices (301) proved counterproductive and was quickly ignored. The Diocletianic Persecution (303–312) of Christianity failed to eliminate the faith. In 305 he became the first Roman emperor to abdicate voluntarily, retiring to a palace on the Dalmatian coast that became the core of [[Split, Croatia|Split]].

Two-terminal electronic component that conducts [[Electric current|electric current]] primarily in one direction. It has low resistance in the forward direction and high resistance in reverse. The most common type is the [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] diode, a crystal of semiconductor material with a p–n junction, usually made of [[Silicon|silicon]]. German physicist Ferdinand Braun discovered asymmetric conduction across a crystal–metal contact in 1874. The obsolete thermionic diode is a [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]] with a heated cathode and a plate. Diodes are used in rectifiers to convert [[Alternating current|alternating current]] to [[Direct current|direct current]], in radio receivers for demodulation, and as temperature sensors. A [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diode]] is used for lighting and status indicators.

Ancient Greek philosopher and one of the founders of Cynicism. Born into a prosperous family in Sinope on the [[Black Sea|Black Sea]], he left his home after a scandal involving the debasement of coinage, in which ancient sources disagree whether he or his father was responsible. Modern scholars remain divided on whether the episode is historical. He embraced poverty and self-sufficiency, advocated a return to nature and the renunciation of wealth, and lived in a large ceramic jar. Carrying a lantern in daylight, he claimed to be "looking for a man," meaning a wise one, and called himself a "citizen of the world." When [[Alexander the Great]] offered him a favor, he asked only that the king stand out of his sunlight.

American singer, actress and television host. Born in East Orange, [[New Jersey|New Jersey]], she began as a gospel singer and from 1962 recorded hit singles with composers Burt Bacharach and Hal David, including "Don't Make Me Over" and "Walk on By." Later hits such as "That's What Friends Are For" came under Clive Davis at Arista Records. She won six competitive [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2024.

God of wine, fertility and theatre in [[Ancient Greek religion|ancient Greek religion]]. The Romans identified him with Liber and called him Bacchus. His wine, music and ecstatic dance were thought to free his followers from self-conscious fear and care. Festivals of Dionysus staged sacred dramas that were the initial driving force behind [[Theatre|theatre]] in Western culture. In the most familiar myth he is the son of [[Zeus|Zeus]] and the mortal Semele. In *The Bacchae* by [[Euripides|Euripides]], he drives women into frenzy and destroys King Pentheus of Thebes for rejecting his cult.

Polynomial equation with [[Integer|integer]] coefficients for which only integer solutions are sought. A linear Diophantine equation, *ax + by = c*, has a solution if and only if the greatest common divisor of *a* and *b* divides *c*, and then it has infinitely many solutions. Because such equations define algebraic curves and surfaces, their study forms part of [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]]. The field traces to [[Diophantus|Diophantus]], and [[Fermat's Last Theorem|Fermat's Last Theorem]], which states that no positive integers satisfy xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ for n greater than 2, was proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994. In 1970 Yuri Matiyasevich showed that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has an integer solution, resolving [[David Hilbert|Hilbert's]] tenth problem negatively.

Greek mathematician of [[Alexandria|Alexandria]], probably active in the 3rd century. His *Arithmetica*, originally thirteen books of which ten survive, is a collection of 290 algebraic problems solved through equations. [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] called him "the inventor of algebra," and his work gave rise to the [[Diophantine equation|Diophantine equations]] that bear his name. Its 9th-century Arabic translation influenced later algebra. A 1621 edition of the *Arithmetica* gained fame after [[Pierre de Fermat|Pierre de Fermat]] wrote his "Last Theorem" in the margins of his copy, leading to [[Fermat's Last Theorem|Fermat's Last Theorem]]. Little is known of his life; a puzzle in the Greek Anthology implies he lived to 84, though its accuracy cannot be confirmed.

[[Genus|Genus]] of over 700 species of deciduous and evergreen trees and shrubs, generally dioecious. Most species are native to the [[Tropics|tropics]] and are ecologically important in their forests. Species valued for hard, dark timber are known as ebony trees, while those valued for their fruit are known as [[Persimmon|persimmon]] trees. The name comes from Greek roots meaning "Zeus's wheat" and more generally "divine food" or "divine fruit." The oldest fossils date to the [[Eocene|Eocene]]. The green fruits are rich in [[Tannin|tannins]] and avoided by most herbivores, but the foliage feeds the larvae of many *Lepidoptera* species. Pure black ebony comes mainly from *D. ebenum*.

Antihistamine and sedative, sold under the brand name Benadryl among others. It is used mainly for [[Allergy|allergies]], [[Insomnia|insomnia]] and the [[Common cold|common cold]], and less often for tremor in parkinsonism and for nausea. Its sedative effects make it a common ingredient in nonprescription sleep aids, and it can cause paradoxical central nervous system stimulation, particularly at higher doses. Common side effects include sleepiness, poor coordination and an upset stomach. George Rieveschl developed it, and it went into commercial use in 1946. Use during breastfeeding is not recommended.

[[Infection|Bacterial infection]] caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. Symptoms usually begin two to five days after exposure, starting with sore throat and fever. In severe cases a grey or white pseudomembrane forms in the throat and can slowly block the airway. The bacterium's exotoxin causes the symptoms and much of the lethality, and complications include myocarditis, nerve paralysis and kidney problems. Death occurs in 5–10% of those diagnosed. Three or four childhood doses of a [[Vaccination|vaccine]], given with tetanus and pertussis vaccines, are recommended, with boosters every ten years. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] such as erythromycin or benzylpenicillin treat the infection. Reported cases fell from nearly 100,000 in 1980 to 4,500 in 2015, most often in [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]] and [[South Asia|South Asia]].

Extinct [[Genus|genus]] of diplodocid [[Sauropoda|sauropod]] dinosaurs from the [[Jurassic|Late Jurassic]] of North America and Europe. The name, coined by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878, means "double beam," referring to the double-beamed chevron bones under its tail. Its first [[Fossil|fossils]] were found in 1877. Most specimens come from the Morrison Formation, dated to about 151.88 to 149.1 million years ago. *D. carnegii* is among the longest dinosaurs known from a complete skeleton, at 24–26 m, with an estimated mass of 12–14.8 metric tons. It had a small skull, peg-like teeth and a neck of at least 15 vertebrae. Its great size may have deterred predators such as [[Allosaurus|Allosaurus]].

Group of officials from one [[Sovereign state|state]] or organization representing it in another. The term usually denotes an embassy or high commission, the main office of a country's diplomatic representatives, typically in the [[Capital city|capital]]. A consulate is a smaller mission normally located in a major city, and may be in the capital when the sending country has no embassy there. An embassy is headed by an ambassador, and a high commission, used between Commonwealth countries, by a high commissioner. Missions to the [[United Nations|United Nations]] are called permanent missions, and member states' missions to the [[European Union|European Union]] are permanent representations. Under [[Muammar Gaddafi|Muammar Gaddafi]], Libya's missions were called people's bureaus. Under the 1961 Vienna Convention, missions enjoy inviolability of premises, archives and communications.

[[Electromagnetism|Electromagnetic]] phenomenon in which equal and opposite charges or magnetic poles are separated by a small distance. An electric dipole, typically in atoms and molecules, is modeled as two equal and opposite [[Electric charge|charges]] separated by distance *d*, with dipole moment *p* = *qd* pointing from the negative to the positive charge. A magnetic dipole, such as an atom or electron, is modeled as a small current loop, with a moment equal to the current times the loop's area. Dipoles experience torques in external [[Electric field|electric]] and [[Magnetic field|magnetic]] fields that tend to align them with the field. In polar molecules such as water, the molecular dipole moment is measured in debyes (1 D ≈ 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m) and influences boiling points and solubility.

[[Java|Javanese]] prince who led the Java War (1825–1830) against Dutch colonial rule. Eldest son of Sultan Hamengkubuwono III of [[Yogyakarta|Yogyakarta]], he was passed over for the succession in favor of his half-brother, and later an infant, which fed a rebellion. Dutch rule was unpopular among farmers and nobles over tax rises and land leases, and Diponegoro was widely believed to be the Ratu Adil, a just ruler predicted in Javanese prophecy. The Dutch deployed over 35,000 troops against his guerrilla forces. He was arrested during truce negotiations in March 1830 and exiled to [[Makassar|Makassar]] in [[Sulawesi|Sulawesi]], where he died. Indonesians regard him as a national hero and an inspiration for the [[Indonesian National Revolution|independence struggle]]. Dutch colonial records often framed him as a fanatic rebel rather than a legitimate sovereign.

Largest living order of [[Marsupial|marsupial]] mammals, with about 155 species. It includes [[Kangaroo|kangaroos]], wallabies, possums, the [[Koala|koala]] and [[Wombat|wombats]]. Living members are almost all herbivores and are restricted to [[Australasia|Australasia]]. The name means "two front teeth," for the pair of large lower incisors, and members share syndactyly, a fusing of the second and third toes. The extinct *Diprotodon* was hippopotamus-sized, and the extinct thylacoleonids, or "marsupial lions," were the only group known to have been large-scale carnivores. Many of the largest diprotodonts became extinct after humans reached Australia about 50,000 years ago, probably through habitat change caused by fire. The earliest known fossils date to the Late Oligocene.

Generalized function on the real numbers that is zero everywhere except at zero, where its integral over the entire real line is one. It models an idealized point impulse. No ordinary function has these properties, so the function is treated rigorously through measure theory or the theory of distributions, developed by Laurent Schwartz. Physicist [[Paul Dirac|Paul Dirac]] introduced it in his work on quantum mechanics as a continuous analogue of the Kronecker delta. It is routinely applied in physics and engineering to model point masses and concentrated loads.

Relativistic [[Wave equation|wave equation]] describing spin-½ massive particles such as electrons. Formulated by British physicist [[Paul Dirac|Paul Dirac]] in 1928, it was the first description to fully account for [[Special relativity|special relativity]] in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. It implied the existence of [[Antimatter|antimatter]], whose existence was confirmed experimentally several years later. It accounts for the fine structure of the hydrogen spectrum, and it is central to the [[Standard Model|Standard Model]]. Its wave functions are vectors of four complex numbers, two of which resemble the Pauli wavefunction in the non-relativistic limit.

City (pop., 2022: 535,000) in [[Ethiopia|eastern Ethiopia]], one of two chartered cities in the country. It was founded on 24 December 1902, when the railway reached the site, after [[Menelik II|Menelik II]] accepted that the line could end at the foot of the mountains. It became a trade and transport centre linking the highlands to the Red Sea port of [[Djibouti|Djibouti]]. Its economy centers on agricultural trade, including the stimulant khat, and light manufacturing. The city spans 1,559 sq km. Dire Dawa was part of a Somali Region autonomous region until 1993, when the federal government made it a separately administered chartered city, the other being [[Addis Ababa|Addis Ababa]].

British rock band formed in [[London|London]] in 1977. Led by Mark Knopfler, the band drew on blues rock, folk and country. Its first single, "Sultans of Swing," from the 1978 debut album, reached the top 10 in the UK and US. The album *Brothers in Arms* (1985) sold more than 30 million copies and was the first album to sell a million copies on CD. The band performed at [[Live Aid|Live Aid]] in 1985 and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2018. It disbanded permanently in 1995.

Extinct canine species native to the [[Americas|Americas]]. Dire wolves were about as large as the biggest [[Wolf|gray wolves]], averaging 60 to 68 kg. Their teeth were larger than those of other wolves, and their bite at the canine was stronger than that of any known *Canis* species, suited to hunting large prey such as horses and ground sloths. The species is best known from the Rancho La Brea Tar Pits in [[Los Angeles|Los Angeles]]. It lived as recently as 10,000 years ago, and its extinction is linked to the loss of its megaherbivore prey, climatic change or competition.

Unidirectional flow of [[Electric charge|electric charge]], in which the current keeps a constant direction. Unlike [[Alternating current|alternating current]] (AC), it does not reverse. It is produced by batteries, electrochemical cells and [[Solar panel|solar panels]], and it can be made from AC by a rectifier. Direct current powers electronics, motors and battery charging, is used in aluminum smelting, and powers some [[Urban area|urban]] railways. High-voltage direct current transmits large amounts of power over long distances and under the sea. [[Alessandro Volta|Alessandro Volta]]'s battery produced direct current in 1800. After [[Thomas Edison|Thomas Edison]] launched his incandescent-bulb utility in 1882, alternating current displaced direct current in power delivery, because transformers can raise and lower its voltage.

[[Graph (discrete mathematics)|Directed graph]] with no directed cycles. A directed graph is acyclic exactly when its vertices can be topologically ordered, that is, arranged in a line consistent with all edge directions. Every finite partially ordered set can be represented by one. Directed acyclic graphs model precedence and dependency in [[Computer science|computer science]], such as scheduling and the order of operations in a [[Compiler|compiler]]. In [[Epidemiology|epidemiology]], they map causal structures, and they are also used for evolutionary and family trees.

[[Germany|German]] former professional [[Basketball|basketball]] player. He spent his entire 21-season career with the [[Dallas|Dallas]] Mavericks of the [[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association]] as a power forward. Known for a one-legged fadeaway jump shot, he won the NBA Most Valuable Player Award in 2007 and the NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award in 2011, when the Mavericks won the franchise's only championship. He was a 14-time All-Star and led Germany to bronze at the 2002 FIBA World Championship. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023.
